summary.text:
Enfield publishes two officer addresses, so it is email-ready, and it is the most checkable report in the library at the level that matters most: Appendix B prints the actual PWLB loan numbers for all four of the year's drawings — 816653, 871328, 876209 and 880921 — and every one matches our own file on number, maturity date and rate. No other council publishes loan numbers.

The finding is in Appendix C. The portfolio returned 4.15% against a budgeted 3.85%, and the whole of that thirty basis points is a single £10m advance to Central Bedfordshire at 6.50%. Strip it out and the remaining £80.0m yields 3.8545% — the budget, to within half a basis point. Eleven per cent of the portfolio produced seventeen per cent of the return. The weighted rate itself recomputes exactly from their table: 373.356/90 = 4.1484%.

Everything else foots. Tables 3, 4 and 5 foot on every row, column and variation; Appendix B reblends to the printed 4.50%; the balance sheet identity closes exactly at £151.3m of internal borrowing; Appendix C foots and its 4.15% recomputes; §9.2's £220.6m of subsidiary investment and §2.10's £8.7m of Energetik advances both tie to Table 7.

Two further points of record. Sections 15.3 and 15.4 state both PWLB discounts correctly — certainty 20bp below standard, HRA a further 40bp — and all four new loans were drawn at the HRA rate. And Table 11 publishes the ANNUITY certainty curve, which almost no one does; every tenor on it is consistent with our maturity curve once annuity average life is allowed for, down to the 50-year annuity rate sitting one basis point from our 25-year maturity rate. On today's repayment curve the book carries about £200.4m of net discount across 85 of 109 loans.

courses_named: PWLB break costs — mechanics & live calculator
officer.body:
Hi Olu,

Apologies for the cold email. PWLBtoday is fairly new so you may not have come across us yet.

We're built for local authority treasury teams and nothing else: live PWLB rates at both daily fixings, a monthly breakdown of every loan the sector draws, every council's PWLB book priced daily against the DMO's repayment curve, and a training academy for officers and members. There's more — the predictor, the SONIA path, peer metrics, a daily brief — in the brochure at [BROCHURE URL]. We don't sell treasury products, and the data side is free and stays free.

To keep that data and our training relevant we built tools that watch committee papers across every council in the country, so we can see how a council's own figures compare with where the market has gone since. So below are a few thoughts on the outturn report that went to Cabinet on 24 June. You're not being singled out — every authority gets one of these — and there's no agenda in it.

A cross-check first, and yours is the only one we have been able to run at this level. Appendix B prints the actual PWLB loan numbers for all four of the year's drawings — 816653, 871328, 876209 and 880921 — and every one of them matches our own file on number, maturity date and rate: £10m to October 2042 at 4.69%, £10m to October 2035 at 4.41%, £20m to November 2037 at 4.42%, £10m to November 2038 at 4.58%. No other council in everything we have read publishes loan numbers, so everywhere else we can only reconcile totals. Appendix B also reblends to your printed 4.50%, and Tables 3, 4 and 5 foot on every row, column and variation, with the balance sheet closing exactly on £151.3m of internal borrowing.

We wrote because of one line in Appendix C.

Your portfolio returned 4.15% against a budgeted 3.85%. We rebuilt the 4.15% from your table and it comes out at 4.1484%, so that is right. Then we took out the £10m advanced to Central Bedfordshire at 6.50% and recomputed the rest: the other £80.0m yields 3.8545%.

Which is the budget, to within half a basis point. The entire thirty basis points of outperformance is that single loan. Eleven per cent of the portfolio produced seventeen per cent of the return, and without it the year lands exactly where it was planned to.

We mention it because concentration of that kind is genuinely hard to see from inside a portfolio table — the £10m appears as one row among eleven, and the headline rate looks like a portfolio result rather than a single decision. It also sits in a market whose spread is very wide right now: across everything we have read this year, inter-authority pricing over this winter ran from about 4.15% to 8.50%. Gloucestershire borrowed £55m at 4.15% to 4.70%, and in the same months Cornwall paid 8.50% for four days and Bexley paid Herefordshire 7.00% for 32 days. Your 6.50% for thirty days sits high in that range, which is the right side of it to be on. Your own 4.00% and 4.50% to Derbyshire and Manchester sit near the bottom. No council can see that distribution from its own trades, which is why we publish it, alongside the monthly PWLB picture — July was thin, £368m across 33 loans from just 19 borrowers at an average 5.02% — at pwlbtoday.org/pwlb-activity.

Two other things worth a line.

Table 11 is the annuity certainty curve rather than the maturity curve. Almost nobody publishes that, and it is a more useful table than the usual one for an authority that actually draws annuity and EIP debt, which you do — of the 109 loans we hold for Enfield, 36 are EIP and 23 annuity, the most profile-diversified book we have. We checked it against our own record and it holds on every tenor once annuity average life is allowed for. The one we would point at is the fifty-year annuity rate of 6.28%, which sits a single basis point from the twenty-five-year maturity rate of 6.29% for the same day — exactly right, because a fifty-year annuity has an average life around twenty-five years and the maturity curve inverts beyond that point. Sections 15.3 and 15.4 also state both discounts correctly, certainty at 20bp off standard and the HRA rate a further 40bp below, which fewer reports get right than you would expect.

And your paragraph 11.2 — that restructuring was unviable on the year's borrowing and premature repayment rates. On the DMO's curve this afternoon we can size the discount side of that: 85 of your 109 loans price below par for about £214.9m, against £14.5m of premium on the other 24, so roughly £200.4m net. The single largest is the £50m at 1.54% running to 2070, at about £32.4m. We're not suggesting anything follows — we don't sell treasury products, we model no MRP or accounting treatment, and only the DMO can quote a real figure. The reason it is worth a line is that the answer to 11.2 changes with the curve and the curve has moved since the year end. Yours is priced daily at pwlbtoday.org/loan-analysis.

On training, four fit Enfield. Intra-LA borrowing & lending markets and LA Credit Analysis go to the Central Beds advance and the forward lending agreement from September. PWLB repayment structures covers the annuity and EIP weighting behind Table 11, and PWLB break costs — mechanics & live calculator sizes the position above. All 115 courses are free to local authorities until the end of September at pwlbtoday.org/academy, and free accounts for the whole team.

And if you do find it useful, mentioning it to others would help us more than anything. We're small, word of mouth is most of our marketing, and every sign-up helps us prove the need.

Sign up free → https://pwlbtoday.org/
Follow on LinkedIn → https://www.linkedin.com/company/pwlbtoday/
